if you are harsh with them, they will surely cry out to me, and be sure i shall hear their cry; my anger will flare and i shall kill you with the sword, your own wives will be widows, your own children orphans. ‘“if you lend money to any of my people, to any poor man among you, you must not play the usurer with him: you must not demand interest from him.‘“if you take another’s cloak as a pledge, you must give it back to him before sunset. it is all the covering he has; it is the cloak he wraps his body in; what else would he sleep in? if he cries to me, i will listen, for i am full of pity.”’ the word of the lord responsorial psalm response: i love you, lord, my strength. second reading a reading from the first letter of st. paul to the thessalonians you observed the sort of life we lived when we were with you, which was for your instruction, and you were led to become imita tors of us, and of the lord; and it was with the joy of the holy spirit that you took to the gospel, in spite of the great opposition all round you. this has made you the great example to all believers in macedonia and achaia since it was from you that the word of the lord started to spread – and not only throughout macedonia and achaia, for the news of your faith in god has spread everywhere. we do not need to tell other people about it: other people tell us how we started the work among you, how you broke with idolatry when you were converted to god and became servants of the real, living god; and how you are now waiting for jesus, his son, whom he raised from the dead, to come from heaven to save us from the retribution which is coming. the word of the lord. gospel acclamation alleluia, alleluia! open our heart, o lord, to accept the words of your son. alleluia! gospel a reading from the holy gospel according to matthew when the pharisees heard that jesus had silenced the sadducees they got together and, to disconcert him, one of them put a question, ‘master, which is the greatest commandment of the law?’ jesus said, ‘you must love the lord your god with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind. this is the greatest and the first commandment. the second resembles it: you must love your neighbour as yourself. on these two commandments hang the whole law, and the prophets also.’ the gospel of the lord 30th sunday in ordinary time 25th october 2026 reflection a jesuit colleague of mine was working in the inner-city years ago and was asked did he need help. he said something that remained with me – ‘don’t come into these good people if you feel angry or guilty. the city has enough angry people, and we don’t need your guilt. come among them only if you love them’. two loves, one love the gospel today centres the message of jesus on love; on two loves united in each of us. love god, love the neighbour – this is the only commandment of jesus. without this all we say we do for him, is really done for ourselves. no law of the church can be above the law of love. no detail of religious observance is above this law of love. jesus said this and lived it in his life. he never allowed the laws of religion overtake the need for love. human starvation took precedence over laws of not working on the sabbath. care for the sick takes precedence over sunday worship. he was put to death because he put himself above the religious details of the people. love speaks to the deepest in us we want this sort of religion. we admire the people who really give their lives fully to others: in their family, in the neighbourhood and in the wider world. we know love when we see it in action because it speaks to what is deepest in the human heart. the message of jesus is all-embracing and covers all our relationships, both the close relationships of marriage, family and friendship, as well as the call to love the wider world, particularly where the needs are great. lord jesus may your kingdom come and may all in our world know the grace of human and divine love. donal neary sj. arles

kildare and leighlin dioceseand and day of prayer for survivors and victims of abuse friday february 20th 2026 (1st friday of lent 2026) - our annual holy hour for survivors of abuse was held in the cathedral parish in carlow. thanks to all who attended and participated in the service. candle of atonement prayer lord, forgive us our many sins. we grieve and repent with all our hearts for having offended you, for our great failings and neglect of the young and vulnerable. we place all of those who have been hurt by the church in any way into your loving hands and under the protection of our blessed mother. lord, bring peace to their broken lives and show us all the way out of darkness and into the light of your word. may we as the people of god be more fully human, more fully christ-like and more fully your people, that we may see the errors of the past and go forward with renewed hope and faith in christ and in our church. amen. testimonials from young people who engage in youth activities in our diocese. message from bishop denis nulty sunday, february 22, is diocesan safeguarding sunday. it is the first sunday of lent and appropriately so, as we enter the penitential season and seek forgiveness for past failings. in his address at the january consistory pope leo xiv reminded all that “abuse itself causes a deep wound, which may last a lifetime; but often the scandal in the church is that the door was closed and victims were not welcomed or accompanied with the closeness of authentic pastors”. this year we have intentionally linked the ‘day of prayer for survivors and victims of abuse’ on friday, february 20 with ‘safeguarding sunday’ two days later. the national child safeguarding policy for our church is called ‘a safe and welcoming church’ and that is what our diocese is and our parishes are, a safe and welcoming church. the fact that ‘safeguarding sunday’ has become such a regular part of our diocesan and parish life, demonstrates how the safeguarding of children and vulnerable adults has been so well embedded into every area of the life of our diocese, its 56 parishes and 117 faith communities. safeguarding sunday is once again an opportunity to acknowledge and recognise the years of dedication and work by so many to ensure that kildare & leighlin diocese is a safe place for children and all who work with them. it’s an opportunity to thank all who today ensure safeguarding is so well embedded in our diocesan culture, ailish higgins, our director of safeguarding, currently on maternity leave, michele hughes, our acting designated liaison person, the diocesan safeguarding committee, our parish safeguarding representatives, our priests, our deacons and our people, particularly the many who volunteer at parish level, ensuring the life and vitality of their faith community. as ever, on my parish visits, i encourage ministry with children and young people, this is an essential part of the mission of the church. where altar serving, youth choirs, sunday school have returned i welcome them warmly; where they haven’t for whatever reason, once again i encourage their early return. the life of a parish is often defined by the active engagement of young people in that parish. safeguarding sunday is a reassurance to all that being involved in the parish is governed by best practices in safeguarding. every blessing & thanks, bishop of kildare and leighlin +denis nulty if you have a safeguarding concern, please contact: diocesan designated liaison person (dlp): ailish higgins tel:

30th sunday in ordinary time deacon: rev. liam dunne matthew 22:34-40 the lens of love the religious elite continue their attempts to discredit jesus as he teaches in the temp le; they try to trick him by asking which of the laws of judaism are the most important. jesus responds by quoting deuteronomy 6:5 and leviticus 19:18: ‘love the lord your god … love your neighbour as yourself’. all other laws ‘hang’ on these two; they are the lens through which all else is to be interpreted. this wisdom saying can sometimes be dismissed as sentimentality, but here jesus is speaking a deep truth. both commandments are interconnected, ‘like’ one another, and their foundation is to love god with our entire being, ‘heart … soul and … mind’. that means sitting with the truth that god is love and dwells within each person; this is our true self (1cor 3:16). this brings the question, can we cope with this? are we able to open our hearts in awareness to this love, to tap into this divine indwelling? then we can truly love our neighbour as ourselves – not as much as ourselves, but as a complete continuation of our very being. thomas keating once said, ‘we’re all like localised vibrations of the infinite goodness of god’s presence. so love is our very nature. love is our first, middle, and last name.’ in matthew chapter 18, we read what this love of neighbour involves: bringing restoration to the community, solving disputes, forgiving one another … serving others. this is a lifelong task, and we cannot do it alone. cultivating a deep awareness of the source of this love that dwells within, in t urn allows this love to flow outward. this love invites us to open our hearts fully to t he divine, to reject individualism and embrace a radical solidarity with our fellow human beings and with all creation. the religious leaders dare not ask jesus any more questions (22:46); they have been ‘amazed’ 22), ‘astounded’ 33) and ‘silenced’ 34). copyright triona doherty & jane mellett. the deep end: a journey with the sunday gospels in the year of matthew (dublin: messenger publications, 2022).

twenty ninth sunday in ordinary time - year a- 18th october 2026 the question as to whether or not it was lawful to pay taxes to caesar was a very serious one, and it really put jesus in a spot. if he said it was lawful, he would be regarded as a traitor to the jewish cause and the jewish religion. if he said it was unlawful, he could be denounced as fomenting rebellion against rome. jesus replied: “give to caesar what belongs to caesar, and to god what belongs to god”(for caesar we can substitute the stte). this doesn’t mean that there are some things that belong to caesar and others that belong to god, as if reality were divisible into ‘secular’ and ‘sacred’. it means that an obligation to caesar stands under and is judged by a paramount obligation: to acknowledge the sovereignity of god. jesus was implying that there need not be conflict between the demands of the state and those of god. the state has a role, but its power is limited and does not supplant god. from this principle christians deduced that they could accommodate loyalty to the state. as christians we have dual citizenship. we are citizens of the country in which we happen to be living or in which we were born. to many benefits. to its forces of law and order we owe the fact that we are able to live in peace and security. to its public services we owe transport, water, light, etc. to its social provisions we have access to education, medical care, and so on. but as christians we are also citizens of the kingdom of god. to it we priviledges, and to it we also have obligations. in most cases the two responsibilities do not clash. but at times they may. and when they do, christians will spontaneously know which comes first. as christians our first and deepest loyalty is to god. to god alone we render worship. in order things we gladly acknowledge and serve the secular powers, praying that they will rule wisely and justly. culled from: new sunday and holy day liturgies, year a by flor mccarthy sdb
